In this scenario, the modular tanks could be filled outside of the airport premises such that bulk liquid hydrogen storage does not need to take up space at the airport. This approach may also save time between flights if the time it takes to swap out empty tanks from an aircraft is shorter than the time it takes to refuel the aircraft. Universal Hydrogen was a start-up company seeking to develop modular fuel tanks for aviation, but they went out of business in 2024 (Gallucci 2024). This approach, like all LH dispensing methods, is 2 still in a pre-commercial stage and requires further technological, procedural, and certification development before reaching viability. The last step in the dispensing process is the LH arrival and storage into onboard aircraft 2 storage. Companies active in designing and testing onboard LH storage tanks include Air 2 Liquide and Fabrum. In particular, Air Liquide supplied H2FLY with onboard LH storage tanks 2 to run ground tests filling H2FLY’s HY4 hydrogen-electric aircraft with LH (H2FLY 2023a). 2 More recently, Fabrum launched its triple-skim composite fuel tank designed for onboard LH 2 flight, which will be used by aircraft developers AMSL Aero and Stralis Aircraft. In 2025, Fabrum’s aviation tanks were successfully filled with liquid hydrogen produced and stored on- site of an international airport in New Zealand, a key first step in pre-flight testing (Alcock 2025; Fabrum 2025). Hydrogen losses during the delivery from airport bulk storage to an aircraft are not well studied, especially given this type of delivery is still pre-commercial. Once the LH is on board an aircraft, boil-off gas may be directly fed to the fuel cell or 2 combustion-based propulsion system. However, if the rate of boil-off generation is greater than the rate of hydrogen demand for propulsion, the excess boil-off would need to be vented unless more complicated reliquefication or auxiliary gaseous storage systems are integrated into the aircraft to mitigate or utilize the boil-off gas, respectively (Blakseth et al. 2025). Toyota is a well-known company addressing this onboard LH boil-off challenge, specifically in on-road 2 fuel cell electric vehicles. In a system developed by Toyota and used in an LH -fueled GR 2 Corolla concept vehicle, boil-off gas that builds up in the storage tank is fed to a self-pressurizer. The pressurized gas is sent directly to the vehicle’s engine while the surplus hydrogen from the self-pressurizer is diverted to a fuel cell to power auxiliary equipment, such as LH pumps, on 2 board the vehicle. Any additional boil-off is converted to water vapor using a catalyst and released to the environment (Toyota 2024).
